What Drives Late Deliveries? GLM, GLMM and Lead-Time Analysis of Olist Sellers

R statistical layer of the Supplier Reliability & Procurement Risk Scoring project (sellers = supplier proxies)

Author

Supplier Reliability & Procurement Risk Scoring project

Published

October 14, 2026

Question and design

The Python layer ranks sellers by reliability. This report asks a complementary, explanatory question: after controlling for geography, lane, product category, freight and seasonality, how much of a late delivery is attributable to the seller?

  • Unit: one delivered order (fct_orders_delivered, built in sql/03_order_intervals.sql).
  • Outcome: late = customer delivery date after the estimated delivery date shown at purchase.
  • Seller-controlled leg: handoff_late = carrier hand-off after the item’s shipping_limit_date.
  • Olist sellers are proxies for suppliers. They are marketplace merchants, not a buyer’s contracted vendors; findings transfer as method, not as vendor facts.

The models are fitted by R/delivery_analysis.R (run by make report before this document renders); this report reads its outputs from artifacts/r_glm/.

Code 
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(knitr); library(jsonlite)
root <- normalizePath("..")
out <- file.path(root, "artifacts", "r_glm")
rd <- function(f) read_csv(file.path(out, f), show_col_types = FALSE)
s <- fromJSON(file.path(out, "r_summary.json"))
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

96,470 delivered orders, of which 6.8% arrived after the estimate.

1. Logistic GLM for lateness

\[\text{logit}\,P(\text{late}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{handoff\_late} + \text{customer region} + \text{seller region} + \text{same state} + \log(1+\text{freight/price}) + \log\text{GMV} + \text{category} + \text{month} + \text{year}\]

Reading: a late seller hand-off multiplies the odds of a late customer delivery by 4.95 (95% CI 4.65-5.28), holding lane, category, freight and season fixed. Same-state lanes have odds ratio 0.48. Remote customer regions (North, Northeast) carry the largest geographic penalties.

Adding handoff_late raises in-sample AUC from 0.717 to 0.771 (likelihood-ratio deviance 2093, p < 0.001).

Code 
cd <- rd("glm_calibration_deciles.csv")
max_dev <- max(abs(cd$observed - cd$mean_pred))
  • Hosmer-Lemeshow (10 bins): statistic 152.3, p = <2e-16. With ~96k orders this test rejects even small miscalibration: the largest absolute gap between predicted and observed late rate in any decile is 1.9 percentage points. The model is used for explanation, not as the production score.
  • Collinearity: maximum GVIF^(1/(2·df)) = 1.67 (all well below the usual 2-3 concern level).

2. How much varies by seller? Random-intercept GLMM

Same fixed effects plus a seller random intercept, fitted on 94,081 orders from the 1,754 sellers with at least 5 delivered orders.

seller SD (logit) latent ICC
without hand-off term 0.563 8.8%
with hand-off term 0.451 5.8%

Only 8.8% of the latent variance in lateness sits between sellers, and about a third of that is explained by their hand-off behaviour. Most end-to-end lateness is lane, carrier and calendar noise, not a stable seller trait - which is exactly why the Python out-of-time validation finds seller-level scores predict next-period hand-off lateness far better than next-period end-to-end lateness.

3. Lead time: negative binomial model

Delivery lead time (days, rounded) is over-dispersed relative to Poisson (Pearson dispersion 4.61), so a negative binomial GLM is used (theta = 5.48).

A late hand-off lengthens expected lead time by 65%; a same-state lane shortens it by 40%.

Caveats

  • Observational data: odds ratios are associations conditional on the covariates, not causal effects. Hand-off lateness may proxy for unobserved seller capacity problems.
  • Multi-seller orders (~1%) share one carrier/delivery timestamp; they are kept with the first seller.
  • Estimated delivery dates are set by Olist and may embed regional slack, which dampens regional effects on lateness relative to lead time.

Reproducibility

R version 4.5.0 (2025-04-11). Package versions: MASS 7.3.65, lme4 1.1.37, ggplot2 3.5.1, dplyr 1.1.4, broom 1.0.7, pROC 1.18.5, car 3.1.3. See R/README.md.
